source: Sebokova et al. (2026) Psychometric evaluation of the full and shortened WGCTA-II in Slovak university students
finding: Total Watson-Glaser score is reasonably reliable, but the five subscales are not. The published five-part structure does not hold up in a new sample.
numbers: N=264 students (replication sample N=137). 79 items. Total alpha=.691, omega=.846. Subscale alpha .23-.51, omega .49-.72 (Inference .469, Assumptions .262, Deduction .234, Interpretation .491, Arguments .511). One-factor CFA per subscale: CFI .60-.81, below the .90 rule.
limits: Translated Slovak form (Form C), one country, students only. Short subscales depress alpha; authors warn that high total reliability does not prove a coherent multi-part structure.
agent_relevance: Do not report our S0 gate as five separate skills. Use total score or a small set of items; subscale scores from these tests are noise.

source: Sebokova et al. (2026) WGCTA-II shortened form
finding: A 9-item version (5 Interpretation, 4 Evaluation of Arguments) fits one factor and correlates with the Cognitive Reflection Test about as well as the full 79 items.
numbers: 9-item omega=.66. Correlation with CRT-N r=.381 and CRT-V r=.299 (full test r=.329, .298; Steiger test no difference). Replication sample: r=.303 and .307, p<.001. IRT RMSEA=.042, SRMR=.076. Inference and Deduction dropped for poor fit; Assumptions items had negative loadings.
limits: Criterion validity is only r about .3 with another reasoning-style test. Many items had loadings below .30, some negative.
agent_relevance: Most Watson-Glaser items add little. A cheap short gate may be as informative as the long form, but r=.3 means weak prediction.

source: Sebokova et al. (2026) WGCTA-II item quality
finding: Item difficulty varied widely: Inference was hardest, Recognition of Assumptions easiest. Authors attribute weak items to cultural mismatch, double negatives and heavy language load.
numbers: Items with loadings under .25 or negative item-total correlations removed. Interpretation subscale had best CFA fit (CFI .809); Arguments worst (CFI .603).
limits: The cause of weak items is argued, not tested.
agent_relevance: Test wording (negation, culture) can drive scores. Gate items for an LLM must be screened for item-level discrimination, not just face validity.

source: Critical thinking skills of Chinese students: a meta-analysis of individual studies between 2002 and 2025 (2026)
finding: Across 79 studies using the CCTST or its Chinese version, students score below the scale midpoint on every dimension. Discipline matters; grade level and institution type do not.
numbers: k=79, N=8,860. Pooled mean proportion correct 0.426 (analysis, evaluation, inference 0.374-0.461; midpoint 0.5). Discipline order: Medicine > Liberal Arts > Education > Engineering > Science. Publication type moderates (journals highest, dissertations lowest). Grade level and institution type not significant.
limits: Raw proportion correct on a translated test; no student-level controls. Authors treat the uncorrected 0.426 with caution after publication-bias checks, but all corrected estimates stay under 0.5.
agent_relevance: Flat scores across years (no grade effect) fit the idea that the CCTST measures something instruction barely moves. Do not judge a scaffold on small gains over a norm.

source: Critical thinking skills of Chinese students: CCTST test details (2026)
finding: CCTST has 34 dichotomous items in five parts. Reliability evidence is modest: a one-month test-retest of the Chinese version was r=.63.
numbers: 34 items; score bands 0-7 not manifested, 8-12 weak, 13-18 moderate, 19-23 strong, 24+ superior (Insight Assessment 2013). Luo (2002) test-retest N=186, r=.63, p<.01. Split-half coefficient 0.75 reported for one subscale grouping.
limits: Reliability figures are quoted second-hand from earlier Chinese validation work.
agent_relevance: A 34-item multiple-choice test with test-retest .63 is too noisy to detect small differences between agent variants. Use many items and repeated runs.

source: Role of critical thinking in explaining students' academic achievement in undergraduate animal sciences (2026)
finding: CCTST score added nothing to a GPA model built on ACT and high-school GPA. First-year students scored below the publisher norm, especially in deduction and numeracy.
numbers: Model 1 (ACT plus HS GPA) F=68.13(1,103), adj R2=.392. Model 2 adds CCTST, class size, youth clubs: F=17.82(3,100), adj R2=.393, no covariate significant (delta F=1.028, p>.05). CCTST below national average, t(117)=-3.31.
limits: One land-grant university, animal science majors, N about 105-118. Publisher gave no norm SD, so the norm was estimated by regression on percentile ranks.
agent_relevance: Published critical-thinking tests show little added predictive value over general ability scores. A gate based on one will not predict task success beyond plain accuracy.

source: Beyond Static Snapshots: Assessing Critical Thinking Ability Through Iterative Argumentation Processes (2026)
finding: Two established critical-thinking tests (TSA, Ennis-Weir essay test) correlate only about .33 with each other, and the TSA correlates more with number-series reasoning than with the other critical-thinking test.
numbers: N=355 undergraduates plus 33 debaters. EWCTET-TSA r=.33. TSA-Number Series r=.58, TSA-Matrix r=.53. New task: single-round analysis vs TSA r=.28, vs EWCTET r=.33; argument integration vs TSA r=.11, EWCTET r=.12. Inter-rater kappa .72-.91. Debaters higher than undergraduates (known-groups).
limits: Paper text has a typo giving EWCTET-TSA as .033; its table says .33. Chinese undergraduates, one university.
agent_relevance: Different critical-thinking tests measure partly different things and overlap heavily with general reasoning. A gate should use several tests and report each.

source: Beyond Static Snapshots: design note on belief revision (2026)
finding: Authors argue multiple-choice tests cannot capture changing a position after new evidence. They use an LLM (ERNIE-4) to code evidence added per revision.
numbers: Eight passages with 11 evidence units; three human raters coded reasons; LLM coding of newly added evidence (their Appendix B, not read).
limits: LLM coding agreement figures not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Belief revision after new evidence is a testable behaviour; relevant to our guardrail that revision must cite real output.

source: The Nature and Measure of Critical Thinking: The PACIER Framework and Assessment (2025)
finding: A new computer-based six-facet test reaches high reliability per sitting in 11-year-olds, but it was funded by the test publisher.
numbers: N=700 UAE middle-school students tested five times in a year. Per-sitting reliability .845, .884, .934, .966, .906. Six facets: problem solving, analysis, creative thinking, interpretation, evaluation, reasoning.
limits: Funded by Macat, the company behind the test. Reliability reported by developers. Children, not adults.
agent_relevance: Tests can be made reliable with many items and IRT scoring. Lesson for our logs: more items per construct, repeated measures.

source: Does Inquiry-Based Learning Improve Students' Critical Thinking? A Meta-Analysis Accounting for Control Group Variations (2026)
finding: Inquiry teaching shows a very large average effect on critical-thinking scores, but results vary hugely and depend on what the control group did.
numbers: 57 studies from 51 articles, 2015-2025. g=1.336, 95% CI [1.061, 1.611]. I2=92.09%. Control-group type moderates (Qm=5.21, p=.022): larger vs teacher-centred control, smaller vs other student-centred. Subject (p=.698), level (p=.774), country (p=.650) not moderators.
limits: g=1.3 is far above older meta-analyses (about 0.3, from memory). Likely inflated by small studies, home-made tests and publication bias; the paper's bias checks were not read.
agent_relevance: Treat large reported gains in critical-thinking instruction with doubt. Our gate should compare against an active control (plain prompting), not a weak one.

source: Huber & Kuncel (2016) Does college teach critical thinking? A meta-analysis
finding: From memory, not opened (publisher page returned 403): college instruction raises critical-thinking test scores by a moderate amount, with larger gains from courses that teach it directly.
numbers: Recalled: about 71 studies; overall effect near d=0.3 for instruction (unverified).
limits: Figures unverified. Do not cite without checking the paper.
agent_relevance: Baseline for how much trained humans gain on these tests; a sane target for any agent-improvement claim.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for teaching students to think critically: a meta-analysis
finding: From memory, not opened: average effect around g=0.3, with dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring raising it.
numbers: Recalled: several hundred effect sizes, g about 0.3 (unverified).
limits: Not opened; numbers unverified.
agent_relevance: Moderators (dialogue, real problems, mentoring) map loosely to critique by another voice and grounding in real output.

source: Arum & Roksa (2011) Academically Adrift; Klein et al. (2007) The Collegiate Learning Assessment: Facts and Fantasies
finding: From memory: large longitudinal CLA study reported weak gains in critical thinking over four years of college; later work criticised low-stakes testing and low student effort. Only the Klein 2007 title was seen (in a reference list).
numbers: Recalled: about 45% no significant gain after 2 years, about 36% after 4 (unverified).
limits: Not opened. Criticism about motivation is also from memory.
agent_relevance: Low-stakes motivation affects test scores. Our logs should not mistake a lazy answer for a low-skill answer.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: On a custom Cognitive Reflection Test, early GPT models fell for the intuitive trap more than humans. ChatGPT and GPT-4 then avoided it.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks plus 50 semantic illusions; 500 Prolific humans (45 excluded). Humans: 38% correct on CRT, 55% intuitive. GPT-3-davinci-003: 5% correct, 80% intuitive. ChatGPT-3.5: 59% correct, 15% intuitive. ChatGPT-4: 96% correct, 0% intuitive. Semantic illusions: humans 26% correct; davinci-003 18%; ChatGPT-3.5 74%; ChatGPT-4 88%.
limits: Custom variants, but similar items may be in training data; the authors say exposure to similar items rapidly boosts accuracy. Early models may fail from poor comprehension too.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trap tests are saturated by current models, so they cannot serve as an S0 gate for strong models; they remain a floor check for weak or small models.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) chain-of-thought manipulation
finding: Writing out reasoning matters for older models; ChatGPT models solve most CRT items even when forced to answer without it.
numbers: davinci-003 with 'Let's use algebra': correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. ChatGPT-3.5 without reasoning: correct changed 4 points (p=.49). ChatGPT-4 without reasoning: intuitive 0% to 10%, correct 95% to 88% (p<.05). Reasoning appeared by default in 97% of ChatGPT-3.5 and 85% of ChatGPT-4 answers.
limits: Reasoning was blocked by prompt instruction; hidden computation may remain.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: a think-carefully prompt is a limited fix, and models differ in how much they need explicit steps.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) few-shot practice effect
finding: Showing worked examples of the same trap type quickly fixes it, as repeated practice with the test does for people.
numbers: davinci-003, CRT Type 2: 2% to 92% after two examples. Type 3: 12% to 92% after seven. Semantic illusions: 18% with no examples to over 64% with 10 or more; the line 'Think carefully and check the question for invalid assumptions' alone raised 18% to 54% (p<.001).
limits: Same-type items are very similar, so this tests pattern learning more than reasoning.
agent_relevance: Contamination or similar training items can make a model look like it reasons. Gate items should be fresh and varied.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023) human norm check
finding: The custom item set gave human scores close to earlier studies, so items are not unusually easy or hard.
numbers: Humans 38% correct vs 41% in original study (n=3,428): difference 3 points, chi2=3.60, p=.06. Semantic illusions 64% intuitive vs 52% in original (n=61), p=.12.
limits: Prolific participants; 45 of 500 excluded for using outside help.
agent_relevance: A matching human baseline is needed before an LLM score means anything. Our logs need a human reference per item.

source: Evaluation of OpenAI o1: Opportunities and Challenges of AGI (2024), Ennis-Weir section
finding: o1-preview was given the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test and scored at about the level of instructed students.
numbers: Ennis-Weir mean 2.25 (81.25%), SD 0.43, median 2; six paragraphs +2, two +3, none negative. Human ranges cited: typical 37.5-62.5%; pre means 43.57% and 15.30%, post means 71.42% and 87.60%.
limits: Single run, one instrument, no inter-rater reliability, human numbers from a few published studies, ChatGPT interface used. Percentage claims inconsistent across sections. Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read.
agent_relevance: The only LLM score on an Ennis-style test seen so far. Weak evidence; rerun with blind expert raters and several samples.

source: Evaluation of OpenAI o1 (2024), other human tests
finding: On several human tests o1-preview beat student means, but trailed on matrix-style reasoning and finance experts.
numbers: Algorithmic Thinking Test for Adults 25/25 vs 19.9 experts and 21.2 best humans. Bebras-based tests 9.75/13 vs 8.03 undergraduates. Lake Urmia vignette 45.5 vs 20.08 undergrads, 14.17 grads. Psychology students beat o1 on text-encoded Raven's. FINAQ: 15-20% below experts.
limits: Same reliability concerns; single model, single run.
agent_relevance: Models do best on verbal and rule-based tests, worst on abstract matrices. Choose gate items that cover the weak side.

source: Not Too Short, Not Too Long: How LLM Response Length Shapes People's Critical Thinking in Error Detection (2026)
finding: Using Watson-Glaser-style items, people checking GPT-5 answers were fooled by planted errors in most conditions; medium-length answers helped most.
numbers: N=24 adults, within-subjects. 15 items (3 from each of 5 categories); 8 LLM outputs correct, 7 with planted errors in the conclusion. Outputs 42-150 words. Accuracy when LLM correct 71-81%; when LLM wrong 25-54% (medium 54%, short 25%, long 31%).
limits: Workshop paper, small sample, no no-AI control, length not manipulated independently of content. People judged LLM output rather than solving the items alone.
agent_relevance: A judge reading a plausible wrong answer often agrees with it. Supports G5: judges should not see the proposed answer, and length should be normalised.

source: Investigating the Effects of LLM Use on Critical Thinking Under Time Constraints (2026)
finding: LLM help raises a performance-style critical-thinking score under time pressure and lowers it when there is enough time.
numbers: N=393, between-subjects. 4 access timings (early, continuous, late, none) x 2 time conditions. LLM from the start helped when time was insufficient and hurt when sufficient. Human-vs-LLM grading agreement ICC(2,1) 0.70-0.82 on counts; 94.7% agreement, mean kappa 0.76 on 100 participants. Under sufficient time, early or continuous LLM access reduced recall.
limits: Abstract and method sections read; interaction effect sizes not extracted. Task follows the CLA-style performance-task framework, not a multiple-choice test.
agent_relevance: Whether outside help pays off depends on time budget. Echoes our rule on budgeted doubt.

source: Cross-linguistic patterns of cognitive biases in large language models: English, Hebrew and Russian (2026)
finding: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini beat humans on a rule-based deduction task but copied human errors on heuristic tasks, and results changed with language.
numbers: 2,028 observations: 507 human, 1,521 LLM. Tasks: availability heuristic, confirmation bias (Wason selection). Chi-square, Bonferroni post hoc, Firth logistic regression. LLMs beat humans on the deductive task; bias-like errors on heuristic tasks; effects varied by language and model.
limits: Per-model percentages not extracted. Only two bias families. Version read is a corrected article.
agent_relevance: Gate scores in English may not transfer to other languages. Test in each language the agent will use.

source: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills (2025)
finding: Scoring student essays for critical-thinking subskills: a fine-tuned small model beat GPT-5 prompting, and no model reached human reliability on unseen subskills.
numbers: 4,115-essay corpus; 500 human-coded (12%). Six subskills, five levels. Llama 3.1 8B fine-tune: accuracy .604, RMSE .933, Krippendorff alpha .606. ModernBERT fine-tune .563. GPT-5 zero-shot .543, few-shot .532. Unseen-subskill accuracy as low as .39-.56, alpha under the .60 threshold.
limits: Essays from grades 6-12; top level 'Exemplifying' in under 1-4% of essays. Exploratory work.
agent_relevance: LLM judging of reasoning quality is only about 55% accurate. Do not use an LLM judge as the S0 gate without a code check.

source: Toward LLM-Supported Automated Assessment of Critical Thinking Subskills (2025), human coder reliability
finding: Even trained humans struggle to agree on critical-thinking subskill levels.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha group 1: Drawing Conclusions .57, Using Counterarguments .68, Using Facts and Opinions .70, Evaluating Evidence 1.00. Group 2 weighted kappa .55-.87. Two coding rounds needed; 200 essays double-coded.
limits: Reliability threshold set by the authors at alpha .60, lower than usual.
agent_relevance: The ceiling for any rubric-based critical-thinking gate is human agreement, which is low for subtle distinctions.

source: When Thinking Is Outsourced: Cognitive Offloading and the Heterogeneity of Critical Thinking Among Chinese University Students (2026)
finding: Self-reported critical-thinking gains from generative-AI use depended on motivation more than depth of use; deeper use went with more dependence.
numbers: N=353. Four user profiles from 25.2% simple Q&A users to 15.6% critical co-thinkers. Learning motivation beta=.42 for gains and -.35 for autonomy relinquishment; offloading depth beta=.25 for relinquishment. 25.8% high-depth, high-dependence.
limits: All self-report. Cross-sectional. China only.
agent_relevance: Self-rated skill is a poor measure; use performance items rather than asking the agent or user how well it thought.

source: Application of AI-Generated Content in Medical Education: Systematic Review of the Impact on Critical Thinking (2026)
finding: Qualitative review: generative AI speeds learning but may cause mental inertia; safeguards include having students assess AI limits.
numbers: PRISMA, PubMed only, English, Nov 2022 to Jun 2025, two screeners; no pooled effect sizes.
limits: One database, qualitative synthesis only.
agent_relevance: Little quantitative evidence on how LLM aids change measured critical thinking; our own experiments would add data.

source: Synthesis of 2025-26 psychometric findings on critical-thinking tests (WGCTA, CCTST, TSA, EWCTET)
finding: Across recent studies, subscales are unreliable, tests overlap with general reasoning, and added prediction beyond ability is near zero.
numbers: WGCTA subscale alpha .23-.51; EWCTET-TSA r=.33; WGCTA-CRT r about .30; CCTST test-retest r=.63; CCTST added 0.001 to adjusted R2 (.392 to .393).
limits: Our own summary of the lines above; mixed countries and forms; not a formal pooled analysis.
agent_relevance: Build the gate from many fresh items, report overall accuracy only, and keep a plain-prompting arm for comparison.
